plan.topic: Tirzepatide shot: does where you inject matter? The Instructions for Use's injection sites (abdomen, thigh, upper arm), why rotating sites is advised, and when a lump that won't settle is worth showing your prescriber
plan.angle: Answer within 10 s, quoting the pen's IFU word for word: you can inject in your stomach area or thigh, and someone else should give the shot if you use the back of the upper arm. The IFU also says to change (rotate) the injection site each week. Quote its exact wording, including any distance-from-belly-button line, and don't coach technique beyond it. New fact, the same figure as L1: in the trials, injection site reactions were reported in about 6 to 8 in 100 people on tirzepatide vs 2 in 100 on placebo. Red flags as our own lines: spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever means calling your prescriber. In the label's wording, swelling of the face, lips or throat, or trouble breathing, means emergency care via your local emergency number. Include all the required safety lines and the closing line, with no Exp F line. Related-video target: L1 if it's verified live, otherwise Side Effects.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Shot: Does Where You Inject Matter? #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1: feeds the new injection-site long-form through the owner-set related-video link (Exp G), with a fresh, high-intent practical question from the injection-site demand cluster. | fact-check: Fine as an IFU-only funnel Short. The Zepbound single-dose pen IFU doesn't simply list 'back of the upper arm' as a site. It says the upper arm injection should be given by another person (a caregiver), and it describes rotation as choosing a different site within the area each week. Paraphrasing 'stomach, thigh and upper arm' without that caregiver detail would misstate the IFU. The vial and KwikPen IFUs have their own wording, so name the device or quote words they share. The ISR rate has to match L1 exactly (DailyMed label: 6–8% across dose arms vs 2% placebo). This Short is a spin-off of L1 and overlaps it heavily. Keep the 'where' question as the single focus so it isn't repetitive.

package.title: Tirzepatide Injection Sites: Does It Matter? #shorts
package.description:
Stomach, thigh or the back of your upper arm (another person should give that one): the label says the medicine reaches similar levels in your blood from all three. Rotate your injection site with each weekly dose.

Lump that won't go away, spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever? Call your prescriber. Swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or problems breathing or swallowing? The label says stop using it and get medical help right away. Call your local emergency number.
Otherwise, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Source: ZEPBOUND (tirzepatide) Prescribing Information, Medication Guide and Instructions for Use, revised 8/2026 (DailyMed): https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=487cd7e7-434c-4925-99fa-aa80b1cc776b

social.instagram_caption:
"Does it matter where I inject?"

Short answer: for how much medicine reaches your blood, the label says the stomach, thigh and back of the upper arm all give similar levels. The label still asks you to switch sites, though.

Here's what the label actually says:
• You (or someone helping you) can inject into the stomach or thigh
• The back of the upper arm needs another person to give it
• Rotate your injection site with every weekly dose
• Injection site reactions were reported in about 6–8 per 100 people on tirzepatide, depending on dose, vs 2 per 100 on placebo in the label's weight-loss trials

One thing to watch for: a lump that won't settle, spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever — that's worth a call to your prescriber. Swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing, means stop and get medical help right away. Call your local emergency number.

Otherwise, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Save this for your next dose day.

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the Short against the current Zepbound label on DailyMed (revised 8/2026), and the science holds up.
- Section 12.3 says, word for word: "Similar exposure was achieved with subcutaneous administration of tirzepatide in the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm."
- Table 1 (weight-reduction trials) gives injection site reactions of 6% at 5 mg, 8% at 10 mg and 8% at 15 mg, against 2% on placebo. "About six to eight in a hundred versus two in a hundred" is right.
- Section 2.4 confirms stomach or thigh, with the back of the upper arm given by another person, and rotating sites with each dose.
- A search of Lilly's Medication Guide shows "Stop using ZEPBOUND and get medical help right away" for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat and for problems breathing or swallowing.
- The title's question gets an honest answer: the site doesn't change how much medicine reaches the blood. Safety lines are in the right order (don't-stop line, then "Not personal advice", then the prescriber line last), the emergency line works in all markets, there's no dosing advice, and the Short is well under 170 words.

Three minor fixes:
1. s2 and s4: the quote cards put Instructions for Use wording in quotation marks. I couldn't open the pen Instructions for Use PDF (it wouldn't parse). A search snippet suggests the s2 wording is "can", not "may", so neither quote is confirmed word for word.
2. s5: the stat label says "all doses", but the numbers are given per dose.
3. s3: the narration and on-screen text say "three sites" but leave out that the arm is the back of the upper arm and needs a helper, which a muted viewer would miss.

issues.claim: Quote card: "You or another person may inject the medicine in your stomach (abdomen) or thigh. Another person should give you the injection in the back of your upper arm." (Zepbound single-dose pen, Instructions for Use)
issues.problem: I couldn't get this exact printed wording from the Instructions for Use PDF. A search snippet suggests the IFU says "can inject", not "may inject". Only exact printed words can go in quotation marks. The meaning is right, and section 2.4 of the Prescribing Information (verified on DailyMed) says the same thing.
